item.title: Google Demonstrates Method to Cut Errors in Quantum Computing’s ‘Magic States’
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it shows a concrete step toward easing the massive overhead that magic‑state distillation has long imposed on fault‑tolerant quantum computers, cutting error rates by roughly forty times on Google’s Willow processor. By demonstrating “magic‑state cultivation” in hardware, the work builds on recent advances in surface‑code error correction and other mitigation strategies, suggesting that logical qubits could be realized with far fewer physical resources than previously thought. If the technique scales, it would bring practical, error‑corrected quantum advantage closer to near‑term devices, though broader validation across architectures remains necessary.

Insider Brief Google researchers reduced errors in a crucial quantum computing resource about 40-fold, demonstrating a method that could lower the hardware demands of useful, error-corrected machines. item.title: Google Quantum AI Demonstrates Magic State Cultivation on Willow Processor in Science Milestone
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks a concrete step toward fault‑tolerant quantum computers by showing that Google’s Willow chip can distill high‑fidelity T‑states with a 40× error suppression and logical fidelity of roughly 99.99 %, dramatically shrinking the number of physical qubits needed for magic‑state factories. It validates the “cultivation” framework introduced earlier this year, aligning with parallel advances from IBM and academic groups that are also tackling resource‑heavy state injection. While the result is still demonstrated on a modest processor and under ideal laboratory conditions, it signals that scalable error correction may be closer than previously thought, opening a clearer path for practical quantum algorithms that rely on non‑Clifford gates.

Google Quantum AI has successfully demonstrated magic state cultivation on its Willow quantum processor, achieving a 40-fold error reduction and producing T-states with 99.99(1)% logical fidelity. This breakthrough addresses a major bottleneck in fault-tolerant quantum computing by significantly reducing the physical qubit footprint required for generating these essential states, directly validating Google's 2024 cultivation theory framework. item.title: Google Quantum AI & DeepMind Demonstrate Modular Hyperbolic Codes for Over 30x QEC Overhead Reduction
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article showcases a breakthrough in quantum error correction by showing that modular hyperbolic codes can slash the qubit overhead needed for fault‑tolerant operation to a fraction of what surface codes demand—over 30× fewer physical qubits in simulation. By sidestepping dense on‑chip wiring while maintaining high encoding rates, the approach directly tackles one of the biggest scalability bottlenecks facing Google’s Sycamore and other near‑term devices. If these results translate to hardware, they could accelerate the timeline for running meaningful algorithms on modestly sized quantum processors, though real‑world noise and connectivity constraints will still need experimental validation.

Researchers from Google Quantum AI, Google DeepMind, and MIT have developed a modular quantum error correction (QEC) architecture that significantly reduces the physical qubit overhead required for quantum computing. This new approach, detailed in a technical manuscript on arXiv, utilizes modular hyperbolic codes to achieve over 30x savings in qubit overhead compared to standard 2D surface codes. The architecture allows for high encoding rates without complex on-chip wiring, demonstrating high tolerance to noise in simulations. item.title: Germany Issues Joint Federal PQC Migration Guidelines to Align with EU Post-Quantum Roadmap
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it marks the first coordinated national rollout of post‑quantum cryptography in Europe, turning abstract standards into a concrete migration schedule that will shape how critical infrastructure is protected against future quantum attacks. By syncing Germany’s three‑phase plan with the EU roadmap and mandating hybrid schemes by 2030, the guidance accelerates industry adoption while giving vendors a clear timeline to certify PQC algorithms. The move also signals to the broader quantum ecosystem that practical security transitions are now a policy priority, though the 2035 full‑migration target underscores the technical and legacy‑system challenges still ahead.

Germany has released national guidelines for migrating to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC), aligning with the EU's roadmap. The strategy, driven by advancements in AI and threats to classical encryption, outlines a three-phase migration timeline, prioritizing high-risk systems by 2030 and aiming for full migration by 2035. This initiative mandates hybrid cryptographic mechanisms and PQC readiness in risk management for critical infrastructure. item.title: FirstQFM Foundation Model Cuts Quantum Gate Times by 33% on QuantWare QPU via NVIDIA Computing
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a software‑driven foundation model can shave a full third off single‑qubit gate times on QuantWare’s 21‑qubit Contralto‑D21 processor while preserving fidelity—a rare instance where algorithmic calibration beats raw hardware upgrades. By leveraging NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and Quantum Machines’ OPX stack, FirstQFM demonstrates that tighter control loops can translate directly into faster circuit execution and even modest gains in two‑qubit Bell‑state quality, a step toward reducing overall quantum runtime overheads. The result dovetails with recent efforts to use machine‑learning‑based pulse shaping on superconducting chips, suggesting that further speedups may be achieved without redesigning the cryogenic hardware. However, the improvement is demonstrated on a relatively small device, so scaling the approach to larger processors will be the next critical test.

FirstQFM AB has achieved a 33% reduction in single-qubit gate execution times on QuantWare’s 21-qubit Contralto-D21 superconducting quantum processor, without compromising gate fidelity. This was accomplished using their patented quantum foundation model technology, which integrates with Quantum Machines’ OPX control hardware and QUA calibration stack. The model, developed with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing infrastructure, also improved two-qubit Bell-state fidelities. item.title: Terra Quantum Publishes White Paper Detailing Post-Quantum Cryptography Migration Paths for Blockchain Ecosystems
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it translates the abstract threat of Shor’s algorithm into concrete migration road‑maps for the blockchain platforms that underpin today’s decentralized finance ecosystem. By spotlighting Falcon‑512 as a compact, high‑throughput signature scheme, Terra Quantum bridges recent PQC standardization efforts with the practical constraints of ledger scalability—a gap that has been largely unaddressed in prior cryptography research. The analysis also contextualizes emerging proposals such as Ethereum’s EIP‑8052 and Solana’s WOTS vaults, giving developers a realistic timeline for upgrading security before large‑scale quantum computers become viable.

A white paper by Terra Quantum AG analyzes the vulnerability of major blockchain platforms like Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) threats, highlighting the risks posed by Shor's algorithm to digital signature algorithms. The study evaluates PQC migration strategies, emphasizing signature payload size as a critical factor for high-throughput ledgers, and suggests FN-DSA (Falcon-512) as a viable solution due to its compact signature footprint. The paper also reviews mitigation frameworks, including Solana's WOTS vaults, Algorand's Falcon account roadmaps, and Ethereum's EIP-8052 proposal. item.title: Terra Quantum and Schaeffler Publish Peer-Reviewed Study on Hybrid Quantum Machine Learning for Materials Modeling
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that hybrid quantum‑classical machine‑learning models can now deliver materially better predictions of atomic energies and forces while using far fewer resources than pure classical approaches, a milestone for quantum‑accelerated materials design. By embedding Quantum Depth‑Infused variational layers into the Allegro potential, Terra Quantum and Schaeffler demonstrate that even near‑term noisy devices can improve battery‑anode simulations such as copper‑lithium alloys, linking directly to industry‑relevant R&D. The work also highlights a practical advantage: hyperparameters trained on one dataset transfer cleanly to new materials, suggesting a path toward reusable quantum‑enhanced force fields. While the results are promising, scaling to larger, more complex systems will still require advances in qubit fidelity and error mitigation before widespread adoption.

Terra Quantum and Schaeffler have published a peer-reviewed study in Computational Materials Science on hybrid quantum machine learning for materials modeling. Their research demonstrates that a hybrid quantum-classical Allegro model, incorporating Quantum Depth-Infused (QDI) variational quantum circuit layers, significantly improves the accuracy of atomic energy and force predictions, particularly for copper-lithium structures relevant to battery anode research. This hybrid approach offers a substantial reduction in computational overhead while maintaining high accuracy, even when transferring hyperparameters to new datasets. item.description:

The result validates a key hardware requirement for fault‑tolerant architectures, though extending the technique to larger arrays and integrating fast two‑qubit gates remains an open challenge.

item.title: Quantum-Aware Key Rank for Side-Channel Attacks evaluation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article fills a crucial gap by giving side‑channel analysts a concrete framework for estimating how much advantage a quantum adversary would gain when finishing a key‑rank search on a quantum computer, something that has been missing from current evaluation pipelines. By showing that the quadratic Grover speedup only holds up to a depth‑limited rank threshold (around 2^58.6 for AES‑128 under today’s NIST MAXDEPTH budget) and then collapses to a modest constant factor, it provides realistic security margins for hardware designers who must now consider quantum‑aware key ranks alongside classical ones. The work also offers a practical metric that can be derived from existing post‑processing tools, enabling labs to quickly assess whether their devices remain safe against near‑term quantum‑enhanced side‑channel attacks.

Side-channel attacks on block ciphers rarely recover the key outright: they leave a residual key space ordered by subkey posteriors, and evaluation laboratories report the key rank of the true key against thresholds near 2^48 and 2^60. No evaluation framework models an adversary who collects traces classically and finishes the search on a quantum computer, although quantum search with advice provides exactly that. We give such an adversary a cost model and a metric. For a device whose key has rank r, any quantum algorithm with classical access to the posteriors needs Omega(sqrt(r)) cipher evaluations, and block search achieves O(sqrt(r)); the per-instance advantage is exactly quadratic, and the super-quadratic exponents reported for search with advice are averages over the prior that apply to no single device. Under the NIST MAXDEPTH budget D and a Grover iteration of g gates and depth d, the quadratic advantage holds only for ranks up to (4D/(pi d))^2 and collapses to a constant factor beyond; with the best published AES-128 oracle and D = 2^40 the window closes near rank 2^58.6. We define the quantum-aware key rank, the classical rank of equal cost, computable from the rank estimators laboratories already run, and derive the classical rank a device must retain to keep a given threshold against each depth budget. Block search and amplitude amplification from the product-form posterior state are within a factor of two to four of each other on Hamming-weight posteriors, so the cost of coherent indexing decides between them. Experiments on simulated leakage and a toy cipher confirm the predicted window: at SNR 0.125 a depth-limited quantum adversary is worth about 22 traces to a classical one, however large its gate budget.

item.title: Analog Cosmology in a Quenched Bose-Einstein Condensate Bubble
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a thin spherical Bose‑Einstein condensate can be driven to mimic the expansion or contraction of a positively curved universe, turning a tabletop ultracold experiment into an analog gravity platform for early‑cosmology phenomena. By quenching the interaction strength they demonstrate cosmological particle creation and Sakharov‑like oscillations in the structure factor, and even propose extracting the entanglement of the produced pairs via logarithmic negativity—a direct link between quantum information tools and curved‑spacetime physics. The work builds on recent bubble‑trap experiments and extends analog gravity beyond acoustic horizons, offering a controllable testbed for quantum field theory in expanding geometries that could inform both fundamental cosmology and quantum simulation strategies.

Recent interest and realization of ultracold bosons confined in shell-shaped, or bubble, traps have opened up several directions in the study of Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) in intrinsically curved geometries. Here, we explore the prospect of using thin spherical shell-shaped BECs as analog gravity simulators of an expanding or contracting curved universe. We study an interacting BEC bubble subject to a temporal quench of the interaction strength. Our theoretical approach, which uses a Bogoliubov treatment following a dimensional reduction of a spherical BEC to the low-energy excitations of a shell-shaped structure, demonstrates how this system serves as a laboratory analog for a positively curved universe having a time-varying scale factor. We investigate spontaneous pair production triggered by quenches associated with exponentially decaying or growing interaction strengths, focusing on the emergence of oscillations in the structure factor---analogous to Sakharov oscillations in the Cosmic Microwave Background angular power spectrum. We quantify the entanglement of the produced pairs via logarithmic negativity, and show how this measure may be extracted from the power spectrum. These findings establish a bridge between quantum information science and early-universe cosmology in a laboratory setting.

Read original at arXiv Condensed Matter

item.title: Geometric-resource bounds and permutation-averaged success probabilities for the WZP algorithm
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pushes the WZP linear‑system solver beyond real symmetric matrices to the fully complex Hermitian case, opening a path for quantum algorithms that can tackle the broader class of problems common in machine learning and optimization. By framing the postselection success probability as an expectation value of a positive operator, the authors derive tight separable, incoherent and real‑state bounds that tie algorithmic performance directly to geometric entanglement, coherence and imaginarity—resources that have only recently been quantified for quantum computation. The permutation‑averaged analysis further shows how coherence fractions control success rates, giving designers concrete metrics for optimizing preprocessing and resource allocation in near‑term implementations.

Solving linear systems of equations is a fundamental task in machine learning and optimization. In this work, we extend the original WZP algorithm from real symmetric linear systems to complex Hermitian linear systems. We then study the success probability of the modified WZP algorithm from a resource-theoretic perspective. By expressing the postselection success probability as the expectation value of a positive operator, we derive upper and lower bounds of the maximal success probability over separable, incoherent, and real pure states. These bounds further establish connections between the maximal success probability and geometric entanglement, coherence, and imaginarity. We further show that, under permutation averaging, the averaged success probability is an affine function of the coherence fraction, with its dependence determined by the alignment between the success operator and the equal-superposition state. We also investigate the preprocessed WZP algorithm under subgroup-constrained preprocessing. For the two-level family, the optimal success probability is determined by the maximal projection weight onto the orbit of the target projector. Our results provide a unified perspective on the WZP success probability under different operational constraints.

item.title: Loss-Tolerant Measurement-Device-Independent QKD over Untrusted Repeaters via High-Dimensional Time-Bin Multiplexing
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a loss‑tolerant MDI‑QKD scheme that leverages high‑dimensional time‑bin multiplexing together with NV‑center quantum memories, allowing each transmitted photon to generate multiple EPR pairs and thereby boost key rates despite channel attenuation. By combining a memory‑insensitive architecture with entanglement swapping at an untrusted node, the protocol directly addresses two of the biggest hurdles for scalable quantum networks—long‑distance loss and the need to trust repeaters—building on recent advances in multiplexed photon sources and solid‑state memories. If the demanding NV‑center coherence and fast routing requirements can be met experimentally, the approach could markedly extend secure quantum communication beyond what single‑photon MDI‑QKD or satellite links currently achieve.

We propose a loss-tolerant measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) protocol using time-bin-multiplexed single photons entangled with local qubits stored in nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers. In each round, Alice and Bob each send a single multiplexed photon to an untrusted intermediary, Charlie. Each photon first becomes entangled with Charlie's NV-center qubits; Charlie then performs entanglement swapping between his NV qubits to establish EPR pairs between Alice's and Bob's local qubits. With $d$ time bins per photon, $\log_2 d + 1$ EPR pairs can be generated per transmitted photon, substantially increasing the probability of EPR-pair creation under limited channel bandwidth. To further mitigate the effects of prolonged memory storage, the protocol employs a memory-insensitive (MI) architecture, where multiple banks of qubits and multiplexed photon routing reduce the effective memory lifetime requirements. This approach enhances loss tolerance, enabling higher secret key rates and secure key distribution over longer distances compared to conventional single-photon protocols. Using the Lo-Chau EPR-QKD framework and Shor-Preskill reduction, we prove that the protocol is secure without trusting intermediate nodes, making it suitable for quantum networks with untrusted repeaters.

item.title: A low-cost compact muon detector for millikelvin operation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a compact, low‑cost muon detector that can operate at the millikelvin temperatures typical of superconducting qubit processors, providing a practical way to tag cosmic‑ray events that cause correlated errors in quantum error‑correction cycles. By showing reliable coincidence counting down to 10 mK and uncovering a previously unseen double‑pulse signature below 8 K, the work extends recent efforts to integrate radiation vetoes directly inside dilution refrigerators without sacrificing performance. The ability to embed such detectors could improve qubit fidelity and simplify shielding requirements, although scaling the approach to large‑scale cryogenic arrays will still need engineering validation.

Ionizing radiation produces correlated errors in superconducting qubits, posing some challenges to quantum error correction. In addition, it causes background events in other superconducting cryogenic devices, such as kinetic inductance detectors and superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors. Cosmic muons are a component of this background that can only be partly shielded against at ground level, but can be tagged by an independent detector inside the cryostat, so that the affected data can be vetoed, or the muon tags incorporated into error correction. We present a low-cost, compact muon detector consisting of two plastic scintillator modules, each read out by a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM), operated in coincidence. We characterize the SiPMs from room temperature down to 10 mK, including the breakdown and upper-limit voltages that define the operating bias range. Operated as a muon counter, the detector measures a coincidence rate that, as expected, is independent of temperature within uncertainties and agrees with analytical and Monte Carlo predictions. Below approximately 8 K, each muon event produces two pulses, one narrow and one broad, an effect that, to our knowledge, has not been reported before. Coincidences with an independent muon detector outside the cryostat confirm that muons are still counted reliably in this regime. By studying the appearance of double pulses as a function of temperature and magnetic field up to 4.5 T, we find a behavior consistent with the phase diagram of a type-II superconductor. This links the double pulses to a superconducting material in the SiPM, likely an adhesion layer or diffusion barrier introduced during manufacturing. The mechanism by which the superconducting state produces the second pulse is not yet understood.

item.title: Advances in quantum optomechanical control based on cavity cold-atom systems
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article surveys recent advances in cavity cold‑atom optomechanics, highlighting how the combination of ultracold atomic ensembles with high‑finesse cavities is finally reaching the ultrastrong coupling regime that was previously only theoretical. By leveraging long coherence times and tunable light‑matter interactions, these platforms promise new routes to quantum‑limited sensors and hybrid interfaces for quantum networks, complementing solid‑state optomechanical devices that struggle with thermal noise. The review also points out remaining challenges such as scaling to many modes and integrating with scalable photonic architectures, underscoring why the field is poised for rapid experimental breakthroughs.

Cavity optomechanics represents a frontier research direction in quantum science and technology, centered on the control and exploration of interactions between electromagnetic fields and mechanical motion. Rooted in quantum mechanics, this field realizes efficient coupling and precise manipulation of optical fields and mechanical vibrations through the structural design and precise regulation of optical microcavities and mechanical oscillators, thereby revealing and harnessing novel quantum phenomena. In recent years, cavity optomechanics has evolved into an interdisciplinary frontier integrating quantum optics, condensed matter physics, and quantum precision measurement, exhibiting profound application in both fundamental physics research and quantum information science. With advancements in technologies such as nanomanufacturing and laser cooling, optomechanical interactions have been successfully demonstrated in various experimental systems. Among these platforms, cavity cold-atom systems stand out as one of the ideal platforms for implementing quantum optomechanics. Featuring exceptional environmental isolation, long quantum coherence times, and strong light-matter interaction, these systems provide a crucial testbed for exploring strong and even ultrastrong optomechanical coupling effects as well as rich nonlinear quantum phenomena. This paper reviews the recent progress in optomechanical control and manipulation based on cavity cold-atom systems. We first outline the fundamental principles of standard cavity optomechanical systems. Then, we describe the experimental realization of linear and nonlinear optomechanical couplings in cold-atom systems. After that, we focus on the representative applications of this platform in high-precision quantum sensing, quantum memory, and the preparation of macroscopic nonclassical states. Finally, we give an outlook and challenges in this field.

item.title: Hyperentanglement in intermediate phase-space planes: benchmarking a photon-pair source for quantum key distribution
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that by measuring photon‑pair correlations in intermediate fractional‑Fourier planes, researchers can preserve polarization entanglement while still exploiting spatial hyperentanglement, effectively delivering two independent quantum channels per pair. The result resolves a long‑standing limitation of near‑ and far‑field schemes—where which‑crystal information destroys the polarization link—and shows that partial erasure in phase space enables simultaneous Bell‑test certification of both degrees of freedom. Practically, the dual‑channel capability could double secret‑key rates for QKD systems without requiring additional hardware, though scaling will depend on maintaining precise alignment and low loss across the fractional‑Fourier optics.

We characterize a source of photon pairs simultaneously entangled in polarization and in the transverse spatial degree of freedom, with the spatial measurements performed in intermediate planes of the fractional Fourier transform. The source consists of two crossed type-I crystals in a non-collinear geometry, such that the transverse variables carry information about the crystal of origin. Detection in the crystal plane reveals this information completely and destroys the polarization entanglement, so that a scheme using the near and far fields as conjugate spatial bases cannot support a parallel polarization channel. In intermediate planes both spatial bases combine position and momentum, such that the which-crystal information is partially erased, and the polarization entanglement survives in all four combinations of spatial bases. Applying Bell and Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen criteria to the same photon pairs certifies both degrees of freedom simultaneously. We evaluate quantum bit error rates and asymptotic secret key rates in each degree of freedom, and find that the source delivers two simultaneously usable channels per photon pair.

item.title: Joint-measurement advantage and finite-time transitions in accelerated detector registers
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pinpoints exactly when a pair of accelerated qubit detectors must be measured jointly rather than separately in order to harvest the remaining entanglement after Unruh‑induced thermalization, providing closed‑form criteria that link the detector relaxation rates and excitation probability. By showing that computational‑basis measurements already achieve the one‑way optimum while separable measurements can fall short under a simple inequality ( q < 1/r ), it clarifies the practical limits of distributed quantum sensing protocols that operate in relativistic or noisy environments. The results dovetail with recent work on entanglement harvesting and measurement‑based error mitigation, suggesting concrete design rules for future hardware that exploits weak‑coupling thermalization models—though experimental verification will still require controllable acceleration or analog simulators.

The Unruh response thermalizes accelerated detectors, but the entanglement remaining in a register does not by itself specify what distributed measurements can recover. We study this distinction for a four-qubit cluster state whose two assisting nodes independently undergo generalized amplitude damping, while the target nodes remain isolated and the environments are inaccessible. We derive the exact joint-assisted concurrence and the exact one-way value for arbitrary local measurements. The joint optimum equals the bipartition negativity, and computational-basis measurements attain the one-way optimum. A polar-decomposition argument, together with compactness, establishes a necessary and sufficient condition for separable measurements to attain the joint optimum and proves a strict gap whenever this condition fails. For assisting detectors at equal Unruh temperature with relaxation-rate ratio $r>1$, joint advantage exists precisely when the thermal excitation factor satisfies $q<1/r$. At finite positive temperature it ends at a unique finite time, while the remaining entanglement is nonzero. For $r=2$, both the transition time and remaining resource have closed expressions. These results identify when joint assistance is necessary within the independent weak-coupling thermalization model.

item.title: Deterministic and Programmable Fusion for Scalable Generation of Photonic Graph States
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates the first deterministic, programmable fusion gate for time‑bin photonic qubits, turning a previously probabilistic bottleneck into a repeatable operation that can stitch together on‑demand cluster states without massive hardware overhead. By using superconducting circuits to nondestructively Bell‑project flying microwave photons and then actively resetting the matter ancillae, the team scales multipartite entanglement to 13 photons—a clear step toward practical measurement‑based quantum computing and loss‑tolerant quantum repeaters. The approach dovetails with recent advances in solid‑state emitters and microwave‑optical transduction, suggesting a viable pathway for building large‑scale photonic graph networks while still requiring further integration of low‑loss interconnects and error‑corrected protocols. Readers should watch this as a concrete proof‑of‑concept that bridges deterministic matter‑photon interfaces with scalable photonic architectures.

Entanglement in multiphoton graph states is an important resource with various applications, such as measurement-based quantum computing and memory-less quantum repeaters. While some primitive instances have been successfully prepared, scalable generation of large-scale graph states with programmable connections remains an outstanding challenge. Fusion provides a promising "divide-and-conquer" approach by linking smaller resource states into larger, more complex graphs. However, its practical scalability has been limited by the probabilistic nature of conventional fusion protocols, which necessitates extensive hardware overhead and feed-forward resources to achieve deterministic outcomes. Here, we introduce and experimentally demonstrate a deterministic fusion operation with built-in error mitigation, capable of connecting small time-bin-encoded cluster states--originally generated on-demand from a quantum emitter--into larger, reconfigurable photonic graph states of increased sizes. The fusion operation is realized by nondestructively projecting pairs of flying microwave photonic qubits into Bell states using superconducting circuits with in-situ programmability. Crucially, the protocol features active reset and reuse of matter qubits during graph state generation, thereby circumventing the coherence constraints of the quantum emitter and enabling the generation of genuine multipartite entanglement across 13 photonic qubits. Our results establish a scalable framework for photonic graph-state synthesis, paving the way for fault-tolerant measurement-based quantum computation and distributed quantum networks.

item.title: On the structure of low-rank PPT entangled states violating Peres conjecture
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pinpoints a common structural source—unextendible product‑basis complements—for the low‑rank PPT‑entangled states that famously overturn Peres’ conjecture, showing that in 3⊗3 systems both steerable and Bell‑nonlocal examples can be generated by simple local filtering of UPB‑derived states. By contrast, it demonstrates that three‑qubit rank‑four PPT states lack this connection, clarifying the dimensional boundaries where bound entanglement can exhibit nonlocality. The result tightens our theoretical grasp of bound‑entangled resources, which could sharpen criteria for device‑independent security and guide future searches for practical quantum protocols that exploit such exotic correlations.

Bound-entangled states with positive partial transpose (PPT) can exhibit quantum steering and Bell nonlocality, disproving the long-standing Peres conjecture and its stronger steering counterpart. These counterexamples, obtained through explicit constructions or numerical searches, raise the question of whether they share a common structural origin. We address this question in the low-rank regime by asking whether known counterexamples can be obtained, up to invertible local filtering, from the complement of an unextendible product basis (UPB). We find that the answer depends crucially on the local dimension. In $3\otimes3$, the rank-four structure of PPT entangled states implies that both the steerable PPT state of Moroder \textit{et al.} and the Bell-nonlocal PPT state of Vértesi and Brunner can be obtained from UPB-complement states under invertible local filtering. For three qubits, in contrast, rank-four states that are PPT across every bipartition are separable across each cut. Moreover, comparison of the product-vector structure of the relevant kernels shows that the known three-qubit Bell-nonlocal PPT states cannot be obtained by invertible local filtering from the complement of any three-qubit UPB. Going beyond rank four, we further show that a known rank-eight three-qutrit state, supported on the complement of a UPB and PPT across every bipartition, is genuinely multipartite entangled. These results show that UPBs provide a unifying structural origin for important low-rank PPT entangled states in $3\otimes3$, but that nonlocal bound entanglement is not, in general, a UPB phenomenon.

item.title: Dynamical Decoupling of Nonclassical States in a Biased-Noise Spin Qudit
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that exploiting a strong noise bias in an eight‑level spin qudit can collapse the dynamical‑decoupling overhead from quadratic to linear, enabling practical protection of highly nonclassical states such as cat and Haar‑random superpositions. By applying tailored DD sequences to an antimony donor nuclear spin in silicon, the authors boost coherence times by up to tenfold and extend a logical spin‑cat qubit’s lifetime to 225 ms—far beyond free evolution or simple Hahn echo. The result shows that bias‑aware control can make high‑dimensional encodings competitive with bosonic approaches, opening a concrete pathway toward more resource‑efficient error‑corrected quantum processors while still requiring the specific noise characteristics of the platform.

Encoding quantum information in $d$-dimensional systems (qudits) with $d>2$ offers appealing new directions for resource-efficient quantum computing. However, protecting the coherence of nonclassical qudit resource states remains an open challenge. Dynamical decoupling (DD) is a well-established technique for extending coherence, but its application to qudits is hindered by the quadratic scaling of the decoupling sequence overhead with the dimension $d$. As a result, demonstrations of qudit DD have so far been limited to low-dimensional qudits. Here, we show that noise-biased qudits enable a nontrivial reduction of this overhead, for example, from quadratic to linear. We perform qudit DD on a model $d=8$ qudit, the nuclear spin of an antimony donor in silicon. We benchmark DD performance on highly nonclassical states such as uniform superpositions, cat states, and Haar random states and measure coherence improvements up to a factor $5$ to $10$. For a spin-cat error correction code, continuous DD extends the coherence time of the logical superposition $|+\rangle_L$ to $225$~ms, compared to $19$~ms under free evolution and $85$~ms with a Hahn echo. This improvement shows that DD sequences tailored to a system's noise bias can significantly enhance the lifetime of encoded logical qubits.

item.title: Cryogenic Multiplexing Control Chip for Superconducting Quantum Processor
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles one of the biggest engineering roadblocks to scaling superconducting processors: the sheer number of microwave control lines required at millikelvin temperatures. By demonstrating a cryogenic multiplexing control chip that can generate and route XY pulses for many qubits over a single cable while suppressing crosstalk, it builds on recent Cryo‑CMOS and integrated‑control efforts from IBM and Google and could dramatically shrink the wiring harness of future 1,000‑plus‑qubit machines. If the demonstrated frequency‑domain performance translates to low‑error operation in real devices, the approach promises a more compact, power‑efficient control stack essential for practical quantum computers. However, integration challenges such as thermal loading and on‑chip isolation will need careful engineering before large‑scale deployment.

This paper proposes a scheme and design of cryogenic multiplexing control chip (MCC) which enables one microwave cable to control many superconducting qubits. Designed based on adjustable inductor, MCC is a non-reciprocal device which generates microwave signals between 4 and 8 GHz and constructs XY control circuit to operate qubits. The effects of filters, isolators, power splitters, qubits and load impedance on MCC are analyzed in the frequency-domain simulation. And in time-domain simulation, the response time, Gaussian pulses, single-sideband, amplitude and frequency compensation of MCC are examined. The MCC can be integrated with the superconducting qubits on the same package at 20 mK temperature stage, and output specific microwave pulses used to drive the superconducting qubits without crosstalks. The MCC can greatly reduce the number of microwave control lines and is beneficial to the development of large-scale superconducting quantum processor.

item.title: Shot- and Noise-Aware Pauli Correlation Encoding for Max-Cut Experiments on IBM Heron Quantum Processor
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that the often‑overlooked “sharpness” parameter in Pauli‑correlation encoding is essentially a hidden shot budget, and by tuning it to match the actual number of measurement shots the authors recover a clear performance edge on real hardware. Their shot‑aware schedule outperforms every previously published schedule across 150 paired Max‑Cut experiments on IBM’s Heron processor, showing that accounting for finite‑shot statistics—and the accompanying noise scaling—can translate theoretical gains into tangible hardware advantages. The work highlights a practical pathway for improving variational combinatorial optimizers on near‑term devices, while reminding readers that further progress will still depend on reducing device noise and increasing effective shot counts.

Pauli correlation encoding (PCE) encodes $m$ binary variables in the signs of $k$-body Pauli correlators of $n=O(m^{1/k})$ qubits, and trains a parameterized circuit on a relaxed loss of sharpness $α$. The strongest published schedules sharpen this loss aggressively and are benchmarked with exact expectation values, whereas a quantum computer estimates correlators from a finite number of shots. We show that the sharpness is a hidden shot budget. Since the expected sign of a correlator estimated from $S$ shots, $\mathrm{erf}(c\sqrt{S/2})$, agrees with $\tanh(0.851\sqrt{S}\,c)$ to within $0.019$, the edge term of the relaxed loss at $α=0.851\sqrt{S}$ approximately equals, up to a constant, minus twice the cut expected from decoding $S$ shots. This explains why schedules tuned with exact expectation values lose their advantage at realistic budgets, and yields a shot-aware schedule whose final sharpness is set by the shot budget. On five G-set graphs with $800$ variables on $13$ qubits, this schedule outperforms every published schedule at its target budget in all $150$ paired comparisons of the decoded circuit output, owing to the sharpness at $1.6\times10^4$ shots and mostly to switching off the regularization at $10^3$; after a classical bit-swap search, it remains the best on average at $1.6\times10^4$ shots. Device noise damps the correlators by a factor $s$, which amounts to a smaller shot budget $s^2S$. On the IBM Heron processor ibm_fez, an all-to-all ansatz of the type used for the best published G-set results compiles to $835$ CZ gates and decodes to a random cut, while our $96$-CZ hardware-native circuit, trained in simulation and sharpened to $α\simeq0.65\,s\sqrt{S}$, retains up to $0.919$ of the best-known cut. For new circuits, a damping and an offset calibrated on other circuits of the same graph predicted the decoded cuts at $10^3$ shots to within $0.002$.

By reproducing a phase shift arising from an invisible magnetic flux, the experiment validates hybrid architectures as powerful platforms for probing topological and many‑body phenomena relevant to quantum materials and fault‑tolerant qubits. The result builds on recent advances in bosonic‑mode control and suggests that near‑term hybrid simulators could accelerate the design of exotic quantum devices, though scaling beyond a few modes remains an open challenge.

Physicists in the Department of Physics at the University of Oxford have used a hybrid quantum computer, made up of qubits and quantum oscillators, to observe the Aharonov–Bohm effect in a quantum simulation. The effect is a quantum phenomenon in which a particle can acquire a measurable phase by traveling around a magnetic flux, even though it never passes through a region where a magnetic field is present.

item.title: Combating quantum noise with AWS: University of Washington Capstone Project
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article showcases a hands‑on university capstone that leverages AWS’s quantum‑cloud tools to prototype noise‑mitigation strategies on real superconducting hardware, highlighting how accessible cloud platforms are becoming testbeds for next‑generation error‑reduction techniques. By integrating hardware‑aware calibration routines with emerging sensing methods, the project bridges the gap between theoretical mitigation algorithms and practical, scalable workflows that could extend circuit depth in today’s NISQ devices. The work underscores a broader industry push—seen in recent IBM and Rigetti releases—to democratize quantum error handling, making it a tangible step toward more reliable applications before full‑fault‑tolerant machines arrive.

Quantum computers promise to solve problems beyond the reach of classical machines, but they share a stubborn adversary: noise. Quantum bits (qubits) are exquisitely sensitive to their environment, gates are imperfect, measurements introduce bias, and these errors accumulate as circuits grow. item.title: IonQ | FIU Secures Florida’s First IonQ Superion Quantum System
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks a milestone for the U.S. quantum ecosystem by bringing IonQ’s latest Superion 256‑qubit trapped‑ion processor onto a university campus, giving researchers direct access to one of the most coherent and fully programmable hardware platforms available today. The deployment dovetails with recent pushes from both industry and government to expand hands‑on training pipelines, meaning graduate students and faculty can now explore error‑mitigation strategies and algorithmic scaling on a system that rivals early superconducting machines in size while retaining ion‑trap advantages such as all‑to‑all connectivity. While the hardware’s raw qubit count is impressive, practical impact will hinge on software stack maturity and integration with existing quantum‑cloud workflows, making FIU’s partnership an important testbed for translating raw performance into usable scientific results.

IonQ partners with FIU to install Florida’s first on-premises Superion 256-qubit quantum computer to advance research and workforce development.
